Most plants are autotrophic. What do they contain for this purpose?
Plants are non-mobile organisms, most of which are autotrophic (produce their own food) and contain chlorophyll for this purpose.
Why may some parasitic plants not have green leaves?
They do not need to photosynthesise
Parasitic plants may not have green leaves as they do not need to photosynthesise.
Into how many phyla are plants divided in the latest taxonomy?
Plants are divided into 12 to 14 phyla depending on the literature; the manual deals with the four basic phyla.
How do mosses and liverworts attach themselves to the surface they grow on?
Bryophytes have no roots and attach to the substrate via rhizoids, which limits their habitat to moist areas.
Which group lacks vascular tissue to move water and nutrients up to the leaves?
Bryophytes (mosses, liverworts and hornworts) lack vascular tissue and reproduce via encapsulated spores.
Where are fern spores released from?
Ferns produce spores that are released in large numbers from the underside of the leaves.
Why can ferns only reach an intermediate size?
Their vascular tissue is not arranged in bundles
They have no vascular tissue at all
Ferns have vascular tissue, but it is not arranged into vascular bundles, so they can only achieve intermediate size.
What is meant by conifers having 'naked seeds'?
The seed is not enclosed in an ovary
The seed has no food store
The seed has no outer skin at all
The seed is spread only by water
Conifers have 'naked seeds' borne on the scales of cones, whereas angiosperms bear seeds enclosed in the ovary.
Why do most conifers not need attractive flowers?
They are pollinated by bats at night
Conifer seeds are mostly wind pollinated and therefore do not need the attractive flowers of angiosperms.
Roughly how many plant species are found in southern Africa?
Flowering plants form the vast majority of the 10 000 species of plants found in southern Africa.
How does the large seed of flowering plants help them?
It stores food that helps the young plant after germination
It cannot be eaten by animals
It allows the plant to live without roots
The large seed stores food that aids the young plant through the critical days after germination, giving a higher survival rate.
Which features belong to the Liliopsida (monocotyledons)?
Parallel leaf veins and flower parts in multiples of 3
Net leaf veins and flower parts in multiples of 4 or 5
No roots and reproduction by spores
Liliopsida have a single seed leaf, parallel venation and flowering parts in multiples of 3; they include grasses, orchids and palms.
Which is the most diverse plant family in the world?
Although not common in Botswana, orchids are the most diverse plant family in the world, with more than 20 000 species.
Which group includes all our trees, shrubs and most wildflowers in Botswana?
Magnoliopsida have net venation and flower parts in multiples of 4 or 5, and include all our trees, shrubs and most of our wildflowers.
What are the two main functions of roots?
Support the plant and absorb water and minerals
Roots serve two main functions: to support the plant and to absorb water and minerals.
Which type of root is very much a continuation of the trunk and reaches water deep below the surface?
Tap roots penetrate deep into the soil, provide support in unstable soil and give access to deep water.
Which type of root is typically found on grasses?
Fibrous roots are typically found on grasses and some other smaller plants.
A shallow, dense network of thin roots with many small absorptive hairs near the surface describes...
Adventitious roots are a shallow, dense network of thin roots with masses of small absorptive hairs close to the surface.
Strangler figs whose host plant dies rely on which roots for stability?
Buttress or aerial prop roots stabilise plants in unstable soils, or strangler figs once the host plant dies.
The outer bark of a tree is...
Non-living and protects against animals, fire and drying out
The living layer that transports water and food
The layer that produces new xylem
The part where photosynthesis takes place
The outer bark is non-living and forms a protective layer against mammals, insects, fire and dehydration.
Which part of a tree increases its diameter by producing new phloem and xylem?
The cambium lies beneath the bark, transports water and food, and increases the tree's diameter by producing new phloem and xylem.
What does the old xylem of a tree develop into?
The old phloem becomes the bark and the old xylem develops into the sapwood.
What is the function of the waxy cuticle on a leaf?
To exchange gases with the air
The leaf is protected by a waxy cuticle layer that prevents excess moisture loss.
Why are most stomata found on the underside of the leaf?
Stomata allow gas exchange and are found mostly on the underside of the leaf to further reduce moisture loss.
Photosynthesis converts light energy into chemical energy; without it there would be no life on Earth.
In what form is all food first created through photosynthesis?
All food is first created as simple sugars, which are then used to make more complex carbohydrates, fats and proteins.
According to the manual, what acts as the sperm cell of a plant?
Pollen acts as the sperm cell; the female part of the flower must be fertilised by pollen before fruit or seed is produced.
White flowers that open at night mainly attract...
Large bright flowers are pollinated mainly by birds and insects, while white flowers that open at night attract bats and moths.
Which of these is a MALE part of a flower?
The female parts (pistil) are the stigma, style, ovary and ovule; the male parts (stamen) are the filament and anther.
A tree species with separate male and female plants is described as...
Some trees have separate male and female plants (dioecious) and rely on birds and insects as pollination vectors.
Why do some plants invest a lot of energy in producing edible fruit?
So animals spread the seed far and wide
So the seeds float on water
So the seeds are flung a short distance
So the seeds stick to animal hair
The energy spent on edible fruit ensures the seed is dispersed far and wide by animals.
Burst open and fling seeds a short distance
Stick to the hair of passing animals
Drift long distances in the wind
Some seed pods dehisce (burst open) and the seeds are flung a short distance from the parent plant.
Seeds with burrs or barbs are dispersed by...
Sticking to the hair of passing animals
Some seeds have burrs or barbs that stick to the hair of passing animals.
Small hair-like structures on plants that may be sharp or sticky are called...
Trichomes are small hair-like structures that may be sharp or sticky and are a mechanical defence.
Which of these is a MECHANICAL defence of plants?
Mechanical defences are physical barriers such as thorns, spines, thick cuticles and trichomes; the others are chemical defences.
How do tannins defend a plant?
Tannins are a chemical defence that reduce protein digestion in the animal that eats the plant.
What do cyanogenic glycosides release when plant cells are damaged?
Cyanogenic glycosides release toxic cyanide when cells are damaged.
What is the benefit to a plant of defences that are induced only after attack?
It saves energy for growth and reproduction
It makes the plant grow taller
It helps the plant spread its seeds
Jasmonates let the plant activate defences only when needed, helping conserve energy for growth and reproduction.
In tree identification, what does 'giss' stand for?
General impression of shape and size
General identification of seeds and stems
Giss (pronounced jiz) is the general impression of shape and size of a tree, often allowing identification at a glance.
Which feature does the manual call possibly the SIMPLEST way to identify many plants?
Flower shape, colour and size are possibly the simplest way to identify many plants.
Which part of the plant is the MOST important for general identification?
Leaves are the most important part of the plant for general identification and are highly variable.
How should you check if a leaf is hairy?
Feel it and look at the folded leaf against the sky
Break it and look for latex
Count the veins from the base
Texture is determined by feel and by looking at the folded leaf against the sky to see if it is hairy.
What tells you whether you are looking at a whole leaf or just a leaflet of a compound leaf?
The position of the axillary bud
The smell of the crushed leaf
The shape of the leaf margin
The location of the axillary bud at the base of the petiole tells you whether it is a leaf or a leaflet.
Why should one leaf not be looked at in isolation?
Leaf size on one tree can vary enormously
Most trees have no simple leaves
Single leaves have no axillary bud
Leaf size on a single tree can vary greatly, so compare several leaves to get a representative sample.
In a bipinnately compound leaf, the leaflets are carried on...
Rachillae that branch off the central rachis
The petiole directly, with no rachis
A bipinnately compound leaf has rachillae branching off the central rachis, and the rachillae bear the leaflets.
Which description matches the bark of the leadwood?
Pale grey, splitting into long strips on older trunks
Leadwood bark is pale grey and splits into longitudinal strips on older trunks.
Leadwood seeds are encapsulated in a four-winged structure, characteristic of the Combretum species.
Which use of the leadwood does the manual mention?
Its ash can be used as a toothpaste substitute
Its fruit is used to treat skin conditions
Its fruits were used as a coffee substitute
Its sap is made into ginger beer
Leadwood makes excellent firewood and its ash can be used as a toothpaste substitute.
The oldest recorded leadwood was over...
The oldest recorded leadwood specimen was over 1000 years old, according to Vogel and Fuls.
Why must guides take care driving over young leadwood branchlets?
Their spines can puncture even tough tyres
Younger leadwoods have spines that pass easily through even the toughest tyres.
How can the marula be recognised by its bark?
The bark peels off in large pieces
The bark splits into long strips
The bark is smooth and green
The marula's trunk bark peels off in large pieces.
Why are marula trees slowly disappearing in areas with many elephants?
Elephants dig up the tap roots
The soft bark is sought after by elephants, and in areas with high elephant numbers these trees are slowly disappearing.
Marula trees occur in woodland and grassland but are sensitive to frost.
Which tree has dark bark that makes the trunk look almost black and often grows in termite mounds?
The jackal-berry's dark bark gives an almost black trunk, and it is often found growing in termite mounds.
Why are jackal-berry leaves browsed throughout the year?
Nutrients are not withdrawn from the leaves in winter
The tree flowers all year round
The tree grows only in grassland
Nutrients are not withdrawn from jackal-berry leaves during winter, so they are browsed all year.
Sausage tree flowers are large, wine-red and mostly pollinated by...
Sausage tree flowers appear in spring and are mostly pollinated by bats.
What is the fruit of the sausage tree used for?
The sausage tree's trunk is used for mokoros and the fruit is used to treat skin conditions.
Why is the knob-thorn often uprooted during heavy storms?
Elephants loosen its roots every year
It grows only on rocky outcrops
Water is readily available in its riverbank habitat, so its tap root seldom goes deep; this shallow root system means it is often uprooted.
Which use of the knob-thorn does the manual mention?
Bark strips soaked in water serve as rope
Its leaves are used for basket weaving
Its trunk is used for mokoros
Its fruit is fermented into beer
Knob-thorn wood is used for fencing posts, and bark strips soaked in water serve as rope.
What do elephants often do to knob-thorns that is ultimately fatal?
Elephants enjoy the leaves, roots and bark, often ring-barking many of these trees, which is ultimately fatal.
The bark and seeds of the large fever-berry were historically used to cure...
The bark and seeds of the large fever-berry were historically used to cure malaria and as a powerful purgative.
Why do elephants browse the large fever-berry even though it is toxic?
It is the only evergreen in their range
It has the highest protein of any tree
Despite being toxic, the large fever-berry is frequently browsed by elephants, which helps clear their stomachs.
How can buffalo thorn leaves be recognised?
Shiny and asymmetrical with three veins from the base
Two large leaflets like butterfly wings
Dark green and growing in whorls
Buffalo thorn leaves are simple, shiny and asymmetrical, with three veins from the base.
The fruits of the buffalo thorn were historically used as...
The fruits of the buffalo thorn were historically used as a coffee substitute.
In Botswana, the buffalo thorn is believed to be...
Bad luck if planted near a home
In Botswana the buffalo thorn is thought to be a safe refuge from lightning.
According to Zulu belief, what does the straight thorn of the buffalo thorn represent?
The straight thorn represents looking to the future, while the hooked thorn reminds people not to forget the past.
How can mopane leaves be recognised?
Two large leaflets with a small vestigial leaflet between
Simple leaves with three veins from the base
Large fan-shaped leaves on spined stalks
Mopane compound leaves have a vestigial leaflet and two large leaflets on either side.
Why are dead mopane leaves valuable to mammals in the dry spring months?
They keep protein levels of up to 12%
They contain a lot of water
They have no tannins at all
Dead mopane leaves retain protein levels of up to 12%, making them a valuable food source in the dry spring months.
What happens to the larva of the mopane moth in its final instar?
People collect, dry and eat it
It is used to make birdlime
It is eaten only by elephants
It is used to make rope
The larva is collected, dried and eaten in its final instar, an important protein source for many people in Botswana.
What does the mopane tree rely on for protection against over-browsing?
The mopane relies on hedging for protection against over-browsing.
Tall mopane woodland with trees of up to 30m is known as...
Mopane varies from scrub mopane (2-3m) to large trees of up to 30m in 'cathedral mopane' woodland.
The sap of young real fan palms can be made into...
The sap from young real fan palms can be made into 'ginger beer', which becomes potent if left to mature.
Which animal plays a key role in dispersing real fan palm seeds in northern Botswana?
The fruit is eaten by baboons and elephants, with elephants playing a key role in seed dispersal.
In what kind of soil does the real fan palm thrive?
Soils with high salt content, such as Delta islands
The real fan palm thrives in soils with high saline content, such as those on islands in the Delta.
What are real fan palm leaves used for?
Real fan palm leaves are used for basket weaving.
How are the leaves of the African mangosteen arranged?
In fan shapes on spined stalks
The African mangosteen has dark green, leathery leaves growing in whorls along the branches.
What colour is the ripe fruit of the African mangosteen?
The oval, fleshy fruit is orange or red and ripens in summer.
What happens when milkweed leaves are damaged?
They give off a milky latex
Milkweed's lanceolate leaves emit a milky latex when damaged.
By birds wiping them onto bark
Milkweed's balloon-shaped fruits ripen and the fluffy seeds are dispersed by the wind.
Why are African monarch butterflies poisonous to predators?
Their larvae eat milkweed and build up toxins
The larvae eat milkweed foliage and build up toxins, making the butterfly poisonous; the non-toxic diadem mimics the monarch.
How does mistletoe get its nutrients from the host tree?
Its roots tap into the cambium under the bark
It absorbs them from the air
It feeds on the host tree's fruit
Mistletoe develops roots that penetrate beneath the bark, tapping into the cambium layer to extract nutrients.
The flowers of the mistletoe are...
Red and tubular, appearing in winter
White and star-shaped, appearing all year
Mistletoe has abundant tubular red flowers in winter, attracting sunbirds and butterflies.
How do mistletoe seeds end up on a new tree branch?
Birds wipe the sticky seeds off their bills onto bark
The pods burst and fling them
Birds eat the fruit, and the sticky seed is wiped off the bird's bill, its gluey coating fixing it to the tree bark.
What type of plant is the leopard orchid?
An epiphyte that grows on trees
The leopard orchid is an epiphytic plant that fixes its roots to the rough bark of trees.
The relationship between the leopard orchid and its host tree is...
The orchid benefits while the tree remains unaffected, which is commensalism.
Describe the flowers of the leopard orchid.
From June to November the leopard orchid produces golden-yellow flowers with brown blotches.
Why has the bladderwort become an insect-eating plant?
To make up for nutrient-poor water
The bladderwort became insectivorous to compensate for the nutrient-deficient waters it lives in.
How do the bladders of the bladderwort catch prey?
Trapdoors open and suck prey in by negative pressure
Sticky hairs glue the prey to the leaves
The leaves fold shut around the prey
The bladders work under negative pressure; when prey brushes the trigger, trapdoors open and suck the animal in.
A perennial sedge over 2m that forms floating mats
A small free-floating plant with two or three leaves
A floating plant with round lily-like leaves
Papyrus is a perennial sedge, often over 2m tall, that forms extensive floating mats along water channels.
Which people eat the tender fresh stems of papyrus as part of their diet?
Among the Wayeyi people, the tender, fresh stems of papyrus form part of their diet.
Which plant has white, star-shaped flowers with fringed edges and round, lily-like leaves?
The snow-flake flower has star-shaped white flowers with fringed edges and round, lily-like leaves.
How is duckweed spread to new areas?
It sticks to the feathers of birds
Elephants eat it and drop it in dung
Its fluffy seeds float in the wind
Duckweed attaches itself to birds' feathers and is carried to other water bodies.
A corridor between two eco-zones that belongs to neither
The centre of a large habitat
A single tree and its surroundings
An area with no vegetation at all
Ecotones are narrow or wide corridors of vegetation between two eco-zones that belong to neither of the bordering habitats.
Thickets of Kalahari apple-leaf are often found between which two woodlands?
Ecotone thickets of Kalahari apple-leaf are often wedged between mopane and camel thorn woodlands.
Which tree is one of the first to establish on floodplains when the Delta water recedes?
On floodplains, one of the first pioneer trees to establish is the umbrella thorn, which grows rapidly in the fertile soils.
Isolated islands in flat woodland landscapes
Rocky outcrops form isolated islands in flat woodland and support flora and fauna unique to their areas.
Why do grasses not need attractive flowers?
Grasses are wind pollinated and do not need to use water or nutrients to produce attractive flowers.
How do grasses help prevent soil erosion?
Their seeds fill gaps in the soil
Grass roots bind the soils and prevent erosion.
Which grass does the manual say is the staple diet for a large percentage of the world's population?
Rice is an annual grass grown in warmer, wetter climates and is the staple diet for a large percentage of the world's population.
Increaser 1 grasses increase when an area is...
Increaser 1 grasses increase during under-utilisation; they are unpalatable grasses with high lignin content.
Which grass is the manual's example of an Increaser 1 grass?
Giant spear grass is an unpalatable, high-lignin Increaser 1 grass.
Do not react to grazing at all
Increaser 2 grasses increase with over-utilisation and are normally found in lower rainfall areas.
Red grass and finger grass are examples of...
Decreaser grasses are palatable, decrease during overgrazing and dominate in good veld; examples are red grass and finger grass.
The presence of many decreaser grasses usually indicates...
Decreaser grasses are palatable and dominate in good veld conditions.
According to the table, couch grass is a...
Pioneer grass that grows in any soil
Couch grass is a pioneer, grows in any soil, has high palatability, low leaf production and is an Increaser 2.
According to the table, yellow thatching grass is...
A climax grass with low palatability
A pioneer grass with high palatability
A decreaser grass of clay soils
Yellow thatching grass is a climax grass of sandy soils with low palatability, high leaf production and Increaser 1 status.
Which of these is part of the grazing value of a grass?
Speed of recovery after being grazed
Grazing value includes leaf production, palatability, nutrient value, digestibility, speed of recovery, seasonal nutrients and distribution.
Why does sweetveld stay palatable throughout the year?
Its grasses keep most nutrients in their leaves in winter
It receives high rainfall all year
Its nutrients are stored in the roots in winter
In winter, sweetveld grasses retain most of their nutrients in their leaves and remain palatable all year.
Why are sourveld soils acidic with a low pH?
High rainfall leaches out nutrients and minerals
Sourveld is associated with high rainfall, which leaches the soils of nutrients and minerals, giving acidic soils.
What happens to sourveld grass during the cold winters?
Nutrients are stored in the roots and it becomes unpalatable
It keeps its nutrients in the leaves and stays palatable
It grows faster than in summer
In cold winters sourveld stores nutrients in the roots and the grass becomes unpalatable.
What rainfall is typical of sweetveld?
Sweetveld occurs in frost-free, low-lying areas with rainfall of 250 to 500mm on alkaline soil.
Which veld recovers faster after over-grazing?
Both recover at the same speed
When over-grazed, sweetveld recovers faster than sourveld; sourveld tolerates mild overgrazing but recovers slowly.
A combination of sweetveld and sourveld
Veld with both grass and trees
Mixed veld is a combination between sweet and sourveld.
What happens to grasses after years of under-utilisation?
They become moribund and give way to Increaser 1 grasses
They are replaced by decreaser grasses
Under-utilised grasses become moribund and die, making way for the less palatable Increaser 1 grasses such as giant spear grass.
How does fire help grassland according to the manual?
It controls invader shrubs that block the sun
It adds water to the soil
Fires help control invader shrubs and trees (sickle bush and sweet-thorn) that would otherwise block the sun from the grasses.
When were natural fires, started by lightning, most frequent?
At the start of the rains
At the end of the rains
Natural fires are mostly started by lightning, so burns were most frequent at the start of the rains.
Why are hot fires in the winter months harmful?
They burn grass roots and destroy the seed bank
They make grass grow too quickly
They add too many nutrients to the soil
Hot winter fires burn the roots of established grasses and destroy the following season's seed bank.
